reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: Factors to Consider
sections.summary: Additive selection depends on soil type, purpose of the stabilized layer, desired soil improvement, required strength/durability, additive type and availability, cost, and environmental conditions.
sections.body: In the selection of a stabilizer, the factors to consider are the type of soil to be stabilized, the purpose for which the stabilized layer will be used, the type of soil improvement desired, the required strength and durability of the stabilized layer, the type and availability of the additive, the cost, and environmental conditions.
key_points: Type of soil to be stabilized
Purpose of the stabilized layer
Type of soil improvement desired
Required strength and durability
Additive type/availability, cost, and environmental conditions
sections.applicability: Governing framework for the additive-selection process detailed in the remainder of this chapter.

sections.title: Soil Types and Additives
sections.summary: General guidelines match soil granularity/plasticity/texture to a preferred stabilizer: portland cement for well-graded granular soils, lime for medium-to-high plasticity soils, fly ash (with lime) for soils with little/no plastic fines, bitumen/polymer for silty sands and granular materials, and fibers for strength/crack resistance with limited workability.
sections.body: There may be more than one candidate stabilizer applicable for an individual soil type; however, there are general guidelines that make specific stabilizers more desirable based on soil granularity, plasticity, or texture. Portland cement, for example, is used with a variety of soil types; however, since it is imperative the cement be mixed intimately with the fines fraction (< 0.074 mm), avoid plastic soils unless steps are taken to reduce the plasticity. Generally, well-graded granular materials that possess fines to produce homogenous mixtures are best suited for portland cement stabilization. Lime will react with soils of medium to high plasticity to lower its plasticity, increase workability, reduce swell potential, and increase shear strength. In some cases, adding lime prior to adding soil cement will improve the workability of the soil cement. Lime is used to stabilize a variety of materials, including weak subgrade soils, transforming them into a "working table" or subbase; with marginal granular base materials (i.e., clay-gravels and "dirty" gravels) lime forms a strong, high-quality base course. Fly ash is a pozzolanic material-it reacts with lime and is therefore almost always used in combination with lime in soils that have little or no plastic fines. The use of portland cement with lime and fly ash for added strength is often required. This combination of lime-cement-fly ash (LCF) has been used successfully in base course stabilization. Asphalt, bituminous, or polymer materials are used for waterproofing and gaining strength. Generally, soils suitable for asphalt or polymer stabilization are silty sands and granular materials because thoroughly coating all the soil particles is desirable. Fibers may be used in combination with some additives to improve strength and crack resistance, but they severely limit workability after mixing with soil. Do not create a solid, rigid, or brittle surface that will lead to reflective cracking of the surface pavement when designing stabilized base and subbase layers for pavements. Each type of stabilization method has limitations and appropriate uses; therefore, create and test a representative mix design for each individual scenario of the planned field operations. Evaluate each stabilized soil layer to establish the appropriate thickness of stabilized soil to prevent undesired effects to the finished pavement surfaces. Include a bond breaker when overlaying a stabilized layer using portland cement. 2-1.1.1 Portland Cement Stabilization. Cement stabilization utilizes mixing dry portland cement powder into the subbase soils to increase the shear strength within the treated layer. Typically, this is accomplished by using a dosage rate of 3 to 6 percent by weight portland content and mixing it approximately 1 to 2 feet (0.3 to 0.6 m) in depth. These are general estimations; the procedure to determine the dosage rate is described in paragraph 3-1 and its subparagraphs. Use layered elastic pavement design procedures described in UFC 3-260-02 to determine the depths to which mixing must occur. 2-1.1.2 Lime Stabilization or Modification. Lime modification utilizes mixing dry hydrated lime (powder) or quicklime (granulated) into the subgrade/subbase soils to lower the PI of the soil to control the shrink/swell potential of the soil. Lime stabilization utilizes mixing lime or quicklime into the subgrade, select fill, and or subbase material to increase the pH to generate a pozzolanic reaction that increases the soil's shear strength. This requires fine-grained soils with a minimum fraction of silt and clay to be reactive and is not effective on granular materials. Typically, lime modification is performed on the upper layer of subgrade, select fill, and/or subbase and mixing is approximately 0.75 to 2 feet (0.2 to 0.6 m) in depth. These are general estimations; the procedure to determine the dosage rate is described in paragraph 3-2 and its subparagraphs. Use layered elastic pavement design procedures described in UFC 3-260-02 to determine the depths to which mixing must occur. 2-1.1.3 Lime-Fly Ash or Lime-Cement-Fly Ash Stabilization. Fly ash acts similarly to portland cement and is used to reduce the quantity of lime or portland cement necessary to achieve the desired stabilization/modification effect. Fly ash is a cheaply obtained industrial byproduct used for cost reduction and can stabilize more coarse gradations than lime alone. Fly ash physical and chemical properties can vary widely. Investigate each locally available product for its applicability to the specific project. Additional information is in paragraph 3-3. 2-1.1.4 Bitumen or Polymer Stabilization. Bitumen and polymer stabilization increases adhesive properties, the shear strength of the soils, and decreases the effects of water on the treated soils. Bitumen and polymers are not effective against freeze-thaw action and testing the durability of the finished product is not possible. Additional information is in paragraph 3-4. 2-1.1.5 Lime-Cement or Lime-Bitumen Stabilization. A lime-cement and lime-bitumen combination is used primarily when lime is needed to control the shrink/swell potential of soils and the treated soil has a low shear strength. Portland cement-bitumen is used to increase the shear strength to a desired minimum strength. Bitumen and polymers are not effective against freeze-thaw action and testing the durability of the finished product is not possible. Additional information is in paragraph 3-5. 2-1.1.6 Geosynthetic Fiber Stabilization. Geosynthetic fiber stabilization increases the shear strength of the soils. It is not effective in controlling shrink/swell characteristics of soils. Installation of the fibers can be problematic in the field. It requires material-specific experience and attentive quality control and quality assurance to ensure proper construction. Additional information is in paragraph 3-6.
key_points: Portland cement: typically 3 to 6 percent by weight, mixed approximately 1 to 2 ft (0.3 to 0.6 m) deep (general estimations; dosage by paragraph 3-1); avoid plastic soils unless steps are taken to reduce the plasticity

Lime modification lowers the PI to control shrink/swell; lime stabilization raises the pH for a pozzolanic reaction that increases shear strength; it requires fine-grained soils with a minimum fraction of silt and clay; mixing typically 0.75 to 2 ft (0.2 to 0.6 m) deep
Lime-fly ash (LF) or lime-cement-fly ash (LCF): fly ash reduces the lime/cement needed and can stabilize coarser gradations than lime alone

Bitumen or polymer: increases adhesion and shear strength and decreases the effects of water; not effective against freeze-thaw action, and testing the durability of the finished product is not possible
Lime-cement or lime-bitumen combination: lime controls shrink/swell of low-strength soils, then cement or bitumen raises shear strength to the desired minimum
Geosynthetic fiber: increases shear strength but not effective for shrink/swell control; requires material-specific experience for proper construction
Do not create a solid, rigid, or brittle surface that will lead to reflective cracking of the surface pavement; include a bond breaker when overlaying a stabilized layer using portland cement
sections.applicability: First-pass qualitative screening of stabilizer type by soil granularity/plasticity before the quantitative Figure 2-1 / Table 2-3 procedure (Sec 2-1.5).

sections.title: Screening Tests for Organic Matter and Sulfates
sections.summary: Organic matter and sulfates frequently have deleterious effects on stabilized soil or its additives, preventing stabilization from occurring; perform screening tests when their presence is suspected.
sections.body: The presence of organic matter and/or sulfates frequently has deleterious effects on stabilized soil or the additives used, preventing the stabilization process from occurring. Perform testing for detection of these materials if their presence is suspected.
key_points: Organic matter and sulfates can prevent normal stabilization reactions
Perform testing for detection of these materials if their presence is suspected
sections.applicability: Governs the two screening tests (organic matter pH test, sulfate content) detailed in the child sections and procedurally detailed in Appendix A.

sections.title: Organic Matter
sections.summary: Certain organics (e.g. humic acid) act as hydration retarders and reduce strength. A pH test (Appendix A) on a 10:1 soil:cement mixture at 15 minutes >= 12.0 indicates organics likely will not interfere. Limit soil organic content to 2% max and minimum pH 5.3 prior to adding cement/lime/fly ash.
sections.body: A soil may be acidic, neutral, or alkaline and still respond well to cement treatment. Although certain types of organic matter, such as undecomposed vegetation, may not adversely influence stabilization, organic materials such as humic acid act as hydration retarders and reduce strength. When such organics are present, they inhibit the normal hardening process. A pH test to determine the presence of organic material is presented in Appendix A. If the pH of a 10:1 mixture (by weight) of soil and cement 15 minutes after mixing is at least 12.0, it is probable that any organics present will not interfere with normal hardening. Refer to ACI 230.1R, Report on Soil Cement, for additional guidance. Limit soil organic content to a maximum of 2 percent by weight and a minimum pH of 5.3 or more prior to the addition of soil cement, lime, or fly ash.
key_points: Humic acid and similar organics act as hydration retarders, reducing stabilized strength
pH test (Appendix A-2): 10:1 soil:cement mixture, pH >= 12.0 at 15 minutes indicates organics probably won't interfere
Reference: ACI 230.1R, Report on Soil Cement
Limit: soil organic content <= 2% by weight, minimum pH >= 5.3 before adding cement/lime/fly ash
sections.applicability: Applies whenever organic matter is suspected in a soil being considered for cement, lime, or fly ash stabilization.

sections.title: Sulfates
sections.summary: Sulfates with cement, lime, or fly ash-stabilized soils can generate an expansive reaction that damages facilities. If sulfate concentration exceeds 0.1 percent by weight, do not use cement or fly ash stabilization without prior authorization by the Pavements DWG; determine sulfate in the soil and groundwater by Appendix A or ASTM C1580. The paragraph also prints: do not design, specify, construct, or install soil cement, lime, or fly ash for soils containing more than 0.1 percent sulfate.
sections.body: Cements in contact with sulfates can generate a reaction that is expansive in nature and can damage aboveground, below ground, and nearby facilities if present with cement, lime, or fly ash-stabilized soils. The resistance to sulfate attack differs for cement-treated coarse-grained and fine-grained soils and is a function of sulfate concentrations. If sulfate concentration exceeds 0.1 percent by weight do not use cement or fly ash stabilization without prior authorization by the Pavements Discipline Working Group (DWG). Use the procedure in Appendix A or the current version of ASTM C1580, Standard Test Method for Water-Soluble Sulfate in Soil, to determine the concentrations of sulfate in the existing soil and groundwater. Do not design, specify, construct, or install soil cement, lime, or fly ash for soils containing more than 0.1 percent sulfate.
key_points: Sulfates react with cement, lime, or fly ash-stabilized soils in an expansive reaction that can damage facilities
If sulfate concentration exceeds 0.1 percent by weight, do not use cement or fly ash stabilization without prior authorization by the Pavements DWG
Do not design, specify, construct, or install soil cement, lime, or fly ash for soils containing more than 0.1 percent sulfate
Determine sulfate in the existing soil and groundwater by Appendix A or ASTM C1580
sections.applicability: Applies to cement, lime, or fly-ash stabilization designs; Appendix A gives the sulfate determination procedures.

sections.title: Traditional Additives
sections.summary: Heading for 2-1.3.1 Cement, 2-1.3.2 Lime, 2-1.3.3 Fly Ash, 2-1.3.4 Bituminous and 2-1.3.5 Combination.
sections.body: [Printed as a heading only (p. 5); its text is under 2-1.3.1 Cement, 2-1.3.2 Lime, 2-1.3.3 Fly Ash, 2-1.3.4 Bituminous and 2-1.3.5 Combination.]
sections.applicability: Container section; see 2-1.3.1 through 2-1.3.5 for each traditional additive's specific criteria.

sections.title: Cement (Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Cement can modify or stabilize a wide range of soils, but the soil should have a PI less than 30 and, for coarse-grained soils, more than 45 percent passing the No. 4 sieve, or the effects will be minimal. A bond breaker is required between rigid pavement concrete and cement-stabilized base (an asphalt emulsion bond breaker is not recommended); PCC slab joint spacing over cement-stabilized base is not to exceed 13 ft (4 m).
sections.body: Portland cement can be used either to modify and improve the quality of the soil or transform the soil into a cemented mass with increased strength and durability. Cement can be used effectively as a stabilizer for a wide range of materials; however, the soil should have a PI less than 30 or the stabilization effects will be minimal. For coarse-grained soils, the amount passing the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve should be greater than 45 percent or the stabilization effects will be minimal. The amount of cement used depends on whether the soil is to be modified or stabilized. When designing, specifying, or constructing using cement to stabilize base material for support of a rigid pavement, a bond breaker between the pavement concrete and the cement-stabilized base material to prevent adhesion at that interface is required. Adhesion of the concrete pavement to the cement-stabilized base results in unacceptable cracking. An asphalt emulsion bond breaker is not recommended because once the emulsion begins to dry and harden it does not perform as a bond breaker and instead causes further adherence problems. To create a bond break, install a layer of #89 stone meeting ASTM C33, Standard Specification for Concrete Aggregates, specifications between 0.25 and 0.5 inches (6.3 and 12.7 mm) in thickness. Then install a fabric meeting the requirements of AASHTO M288, Standard Specification for Geosynthetic Specification for Highway Applications, class I fabric with elongation less than 50 percent at the specified strengths, or install a double layer of liquid membrane-forming compound on the stabilized base prior to the placement of concrete. Do not design, specify, or install a layer of plastic or rubberized sheet material as a bond breaker without prior approval of the Pavements DWG. Do not design, specify, or construct PCC pavement slabs with joint spacing greater than 13 feet (4 m) over cement-stabilized base.
key_points: The soil should have a PI less than 30 or the stabilization effects will be minimal
For coarse-grained soils, the amount passing the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve should be greater than 45 percent or the effects will be minimal
A bond breaker between rigid pavement concrete and cement-stabilized base is required; an asphalt emulsion bond breaker is not recommended
Bond break: #89 stone (ASTM C33) 0.25 to 0.5 in thick, then AASHTO M288 class I fabric (elongation less than 50 percent), or a double layer of liquid membrane-forming compound
Do not use plastic or rubberized sheet as a bond breaker without prior Pavements DWG approval
Do not design, specify, or construct PCC slabs with joint spacing greater than 13 ft (4 m) over cement-stabilized base
sections.applicability: Applies when portland cement is a candidate stabilizer per Figure 2-1/Table 2-3; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-1.

sections.title: Lime (Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Lime reacts with many medium-, moderately fine-, and fine-grained soils to decrease plasticity and swell and increase workability and strength. Consider lime for soils classified CH, CL, MH, ML, OH, OL, SC, SM, GC, GM and the listed dual classes, and with all soils having a PI greater than 12 and more than 25 percent passing the No. 200 sieve. Do not design, specify, or construct lime-stabilized soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent.
sections.body: Experience shows that lime will react with many medium-, moderately fine-, and fine-grained soils to produce decreased plasticity, increased workability, reduced swell, and increased strength. Consider using lime to stabilize soils classified according to the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) as CH, CL, MH, ML, OH, OL, SC, SM, GC, GM, SW-SC, SP-SC, SM-SC, GW-GC, GP-GC, ML-CL, and GM-GC. Consider lime with all soils having a PI greater than 12 and more than 25 percent of the soil passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve. Do not design, specify, or construct lime-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent.
key_points: Consider lime for soils classified CH, CL, MH, ML, OH, OL, SC, SM, GC, GM, SW-SC, SP-SC, SM-SC, GW-GC, GP-GC, ML-CL, and GM-GC
Consider lime with all soils having a PI greater than 12 and more than 25 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve
Do not design, specify, or construct lime-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent
sections.applicability: Applies when lime is a candidate stabilizer per Figure 2-1/Table 2-3; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-2.

sections.title: Fly Ash (Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Fly ash mixed with lime can effectively stabilize most coarse- and medium-grained soils, but the PI cannot be greater than 25 and remain effective. Some fly ash sources contain high sulfates, which in some soils may form ettringite that may swell excessively. Do not design, specify, or construct fly ash-stabilized soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent.
sections.body: Fly ash, when mixed with lime, can effectively stabilize most coarse- and medium-grained soils; however, the PI cannot be greater than 25 and remain effective. Soils classified by the USCS as SW, SP, SP-SC, SW-SC, SW-SM, GW, GP, GP-GC, GW-GC, GP-GM, GW-GM, GC-GM, and SC-SM can be stabilized with fly ash. Some sources of fly ash may contain high amounts of sulfates. In some soils, this may lead to the formation of ettringite, which may swell excessively. Do not design, specify, or construct fly ash-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent.
key_points: With lime, effective on most coarse- and medium-grained soils; the PI cannot be greater than 25 and remain effective
Applicable USCS classes: SW, SP, SP-SC, SW-SC, SW-SM, GW, GP, GP-GC, GW-GC, GP-GM, GW-GM, GC-GM, SC-SM
High-sulfate fly ash can trigger excessive ettringite-related swell
Do not design, specify, or construct fly ash-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent
sections.applicability: Applies when lime-fly ash (LF) or lime-cement-fly ash (LCF) is a candidate; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-3.

sections.title: Bituminous (Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Bituminous stabilization (asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, or asphalt emulsions) increases adhesive properties and shear strength while decreasing water sensitivity. Effective soils typically have < 30% passing the No. 200 sieve and PI < 10.
sections.body: Most bituminous soil stabilization has been performed with asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, and asphalt emulsions. Soils that can be stabilized effectively with bituminous materials usually contain less than 30 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve and have a PI less than 10. Soils classified by the USCS as SW, SP, SW-SM, SP-SM, SW-SC, SP-SC, SM, SC, SM-SC, GW, GP, SW-GM, SP-GM, SW-GC, GP-GC, GM, GC, and GM-GC can be effectively stabilized with bituminous materials, provided the above-mentioned gradation and plasticity requirements are met.
key_points: Materials: asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, asphalt emulsions
Soils stabilized effectively with bituminous materials usually contain less than 30 percent passing the No. 200 sieve and have a PI less than 10
USCS classes SW, SP, SW-SM, SP-SM, SW-SC, SP-SC, SM, SC, SM-SC, GW, GP, SW-GM, SP-GM, SW-GC, GP-GC, GM, GC, and GM-GC, provided the gradation and plasticity requirements are met
sections.applicability: Applies when bitumen/polymer emulsion is a candidate stabilizer; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-4.

sections.title: Combination (Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Lime-cement and lime-asphalt combinations are often acceptable expedient stabilizers: lime first improves workability/reduces plasticity, then cement or fly ash provides rapid strength gain, or lime prevents asphalt-aggregate stripping.
sections.body: Combinations of lime and cement are often acceptable expedient stabilizers. Lime can be added to the soil to increase the soil's workability and mixing characteristics as well as reduce its plasticity. Cement or fly ash can then be mixed into the soil to provide rapid strength gain. Combinations of lime and asphalt are often acceptable stabilizers. The lime addition may prevent stripping at the asphalt-aggregate interface and increase the mixture's stability. Do not design, specify, or construct lime cement combination-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent.
key_points: Lime-cement: lime improves workability/reduces plasticity first, then cement/fly ash provides rapid strength gain
Lime-asphalt: lime prevents stripping at the asphalt-aggregate interface and increases mixture stability
Do not design, specify, or construct lime cement combination-stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils with a sulfate content greater than 0.1 percent
sections.applicability: Applies when lime is combined with cement or asphalt; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-5.

sections.title: Non-Traditional Additives
sections.summary: Heading for 2-1.4.1 Polymers, 2-1.4.2 Fibers, 2-1.4.3 Non-traditional Additives and 2-1.4.4 Non-traditional Combinations.
sections.body: [Printed as a heading only (p. 6); its text is under 2-1.4.1 Polymers, 2-1.4.2 Fibers, 2-1.4.3 Non-traditional Additives and 2-1.4.4 Non-traditional Combinations.]
sections.applicability: Container section; see 2-1.4.1 through 2-1.4.4 for each non-traditional additive category's criteria.

sections.title: Polymers
sections.summary: Polymer emulsions (sometimes referred to as latex), typically polyvinyl acetate-based copolymers with 45-60% polymer content, provide adhesion, stiffness, toughness, and water resistance, curing mainly by water loss. Do not mix them with gray water or salt water for dilution.
sections.body: Polymer emulsions (sometimes referred to as latex) can be used for soil stabilization. The most common types of polymer emulsions used for soil stabilization are polyvinyl acetate-based copolymers. These materials have excellent adhesive characteristics and provide stiffness, toughness, and water resistance. Polymer emulsions typically consist of 45 to 60 percent polymer content by weight and cure mainly by water loss. These materials may be limited by shelf life. Do not mix polymer emulsions with gray water or salt water for dilution. Soils that can be stabilized with polymer emulsions are similar to those that can be stabilized by bitumen.
key_points: Most common type: polyvinyl acetate-based copolymer emulsions
45-60% polymer content by weight; cures mainly by water loss
Limited shelf life; do not dilute with gray water or salt water
Applicable soils are similar to those stabilized effectively with bitumen
sections.applicability: Applies when polymer emulsion is a candidate stabilizer; detailed design procedure in Chapter 3, Sec 3-4.5.

sections.title: Fibers (Non-Traditional Additive)
sections.summary: Numerous fiber types (polypropylene, polyvinyl alcohol, nylon, natural) and morphologies (monofilament, fibrillated, tape) can stabilize most soils, but mixing can be difficult in highly plastic soils, limiting use in fine-grained soils.
sections.body: Numerous fiber types (e.g., polypropylene, polyvinyl alcohol, nylon, and natural) and morphologies (monofilament, fibrillated, and tape) are available. Most soils can be stabilized with fibers; however, mixing may be difficult in highly plastic soils. This difficulty limits the use of fibers for stabilizing fine-grained soils.
key_points: Fiber types: polypropylene, polyvinyl alcohol, nylon, natural
Morphologies: monofilament, fibrillated, tape
Mixing difficulty in highly plastic soils limits use for fine-grained soils
sections.applicability: Applies when fiber reinforcement is a candidate additive, usually combined with cement/lime/LCF/bitumen; detailed criteria in Chapter 3, Sec 3-6.

sections.title: Non-Traditional Additives (Other)
sections.summary: Other non-traditional additives (acids, lignin derivatives, enzymes, tree resin emulsions, silicates) vary widely and generally show little benefit for granular soils. Do not design, specify, or construct otherwise stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils without prior approval by the Pavements DWG.
sections.body: A variety of other non-traditional soil stabilization and modification additives, such as acids, lignin derivatives, enzymes, tree resin emulsions, and silicates, are available from the commercial sector. These additives vary widely in their chemical composition and action mechanism, may be liquid or solid, and are often touted to be applicable for most soils. Research studies in this area have demonstrated that many non-traditional soil additives have little to no benefit for granular soil types. Sandy and gravelly soils are often problematic for stabilization, requiring a binder such as cement, polymer, or asphalt emulsion to provide cohesion between soil grains. Medium- and fine-grained soils are likely to benefit most from the other non-traditional stabilizers; however, these are treated on a case-by-case basis. Do not design, specify, or construct otherwise stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils without prior approval by the Pavements DWG.
key_points: Includes acids, lignin derivatives, enzymes, tree resin emulsions, silicates
Little to no demonstrated benefit for granular soil types
Medium- and fine-grained soils may benefit most, but evaluated case-by-case
Do not design, specify, or construct otherwise stabilized subgrade, subbase, or base soils without prior approval by the Pavements DWG
sections.applicability: Applies to non-traditional additives not otherwise covered; their use needs prior Pavements DWG approval.

sections.title: Non-Traditional Combinations
sections.summary: Combining traditional and non-traditional additives (e.g. polymer emulsion + hydraulic cement + fibers) has shown more effectiveness than a single additive in lab/field trials, though fibers reduce workability and are hard to place in wind.
sections.body: Soil blended with combinations of traditional and non-traditional additives has been shown to be more effective than soil blended with a single additive. Polymer emulsions and hydraulic cements with and without synthetic fibers combine well, as do synthetic fibers and hydraulic cements. These combinations have shown promise in laboratory testing and field demonstrations. A synergism exists between emulsions and hydraulic cement: the water in the emulsion hydrates the cement and the polymer adds flexibility, water resistance, and crack resistance. The use of fibers improves the resistance of the soil to deformation and resists the tensile stresses that lead to cracking. However, fibers are difficult to use during construction as they reduce workability and are difficult to place in wind as they blow around and even be blown completely out of the construction area.
key_points: Combining traditional + non-traditional additives often outperforms a single additive
Polymer emulsion + hydraulic cement synergism: emulsion water hydrates cement; polymer adds flexibility/water/crack resistance
Fibers improve deformation resistance and reduce tensile cracking
Practical drawback: fibers reduce workability and are difficult to place in windy conditions
sections.applicability: Applies when a single additive does not meet all design objectives (strength, durability, crack resistance) simultaneously.

sections.title: Selection of Candidate Additives
sections.summary: Heading for 2-1.5.1 Candidate Stabilizers, 2-1.5.2 Restrictions and 2-1.5.3 Fibers.
sections.body: [Printed as a heading only (p. 7); its text is under 2-1.5.1 Candidate Stabilizers, 2-1.5.2 Restrictions and 2-1.5.3 Fibers.]
sections.applicability: Container section; see 2-1.5.1 through 2-1.5.3 for the full candidate-selection procedure and worked example.

sections.title: Candidate Stabilizers
sections.summary: Selection uses Figure 2-1 (gradation triangle, entered with percent passing No. 200 and percent sand between No. 4 and No. 200) to find an area (1A, 1B, 1C, 2A, 2B, 2C, 3), then Table 2-3 lists candidate stabilizers and restrictions for that area.
sections.body: The selection of candidate stabilizers is made using Figure 2-1 and Table 2-3. The soil gradation triangle in Figure 2-1 is based upon the soil grain-size characteristics. The triangle is divided into areas of soils with similar grain size and therefore pulverization characteristics. The selection process is continued with Table 2-3, which indicates candidate stabilizers for each area shown in Figure 2-1, with restrictions-based percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve, on grain size and/or PI. Also provided in the second column of Table 2-3 is a listing of soil classification symbols applicable to the area determined from Figure 2-1. This is an added check to ensure the proper area has been selected. Thus, the soil is characterized in terms of grain-size distribution and Atterberg limits to initiate the additive selection process. Data required to enter Figure 2-1 are (1) percent material passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve and (2) percent material passing the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve but retained on the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve (i.e., total percent material between the No. 4 (4.75 mm) and the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieves). The triangle is entered with these two values and the applicable area (1A, 2A, 3, etc.) is found at their intersection. The area determined from Figure 2-1 is then found in the first column of Table 2-3 and the soil classification is checked in the second column. Candidate stabilizers for each area are indicated in the third column and restrictions for the use of each material are presented in the subsequent columns. [Figure 2-1, Gradation Triangle for Aid in Selecting Commercial Stabilizing Agent, follows on the page.]
key_points: Figure 2-1 gradation triangle: entered with percent passing No. 200 sieve and percent sand (No.4-No.200 material)
Triangle intersection gives an area designation: 1A, 1B, 1C, 2A, 2B, 2C, or 3
Table 2-3 (table_2_3_additive_selection_guide) gives candidate stabilizers and LL/PI/gradation restrictions per area
Table 2-3's soil-classification column is a cross-check that the correct triangle area was selected
figures: Figure 2-1: Gradation Triangle for Aid in Selecting Commercial Stabilizing Agent
tables: Table 2-3: Guide for Selecting a Stabilizing Additive
sections.applicability: Primary quantitative procedure for narrowing candidate stabilizer types from soil gradation and plasticity data.

sections.title: Restrictions
sections.summary: Table 2-3's restriction columns exclude stabilizers not applicable to the specific soil. Worked example: SC soil, 93% passing No.4, 25% passing No.200, LL=20, PI=9 -> area 1-C -> all four stabilizer types are candidates after checking restrictions.
sections.body: These restrictions prevent the use of stabilizing agents that are not applicable for the particular soil type under consideration. For example, assume a soil classified as an SC, with 93 percent passing the No. 4 (4.75 mm) sieve and 25 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve with a liquid limit (LL) of 20 and a plastic limit of 11. Thus, 68 percent of the material is between the No. 4 and No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieves and the PI is 9. Entering Figure 2-1 with the values of 25 percent passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve and 68 percent between the No. 4 (4.75 mm) and No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieves, the intersection of these values is found in area 1-C. Then, going to the first column of Table 2-3, we find area 1-C and verify the soil classification, SC, is included in the second column. From the third column, all four stabilizing materials are found to be potential candidates. The restrictions in the following columns are now examined. Bituminous/polymer stabilization is acceptable since the PI does not exceed 10 and the amount of material passing the No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve does not exceed 30 percent. However, note that the soil barely qualifies under these criteria and bituminous/polymer stabilization is probably not the first choice. The restrictions under portland cement indicate the PI is less than the equation indicated in footnote b. [Table 2-3 prints the portland cement restriction for area 1C as "(b)", the soil classification footnote, and the equation as footnote (c): PI <= 20 + 50 - percent passing No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve. The 2004 edition's Table 2-1 footnote b (printed 2-3) prints PI <= 20 + (50 - percent passing No. 200 sieve)/4, the form the library computes: 26.25 for this soil.] Since the PI, 9, is less than that value, portland cement is a candidate material. The restrictions under lime indicate that the PI not be less than 12; therefore, lime is not a candidate material for stabilization. The restrictions under LCF stabilization indicate that the PI does not exceed 25; thus, LCF is also a candidate stabilizing material. At this point, the designer makes the final selection based on other factors, such as availability of material, economics, etc. Once the type of stabilizing agent to be used is determined, samples are prepared and tested in the laboratory to develop a design mix meeting minimum engineering criteria for field stabilization.
key_points: Restrictions exclude stabilizers whose LL/PI or gradation limits are not met by the specific soil
Worked example (Sec 2-1.5.2): SC soil, 25% passing No.200, 68% sand, PI=9 -> area 1-C

Table 2-3 footnote (c) prints PI <= 20 + 50 - percent passing No. 200, no divisor; the 2004 edition (Table 2-1 note b, p. 2-3) prints 20 + (50 - percent passing)/4, the form used (10 % passing: 30, not 60); the example says PI 9 is under it, so cement is a candidate
In the example, lime's restriction (PI not less than 12) excludes lime; bituminous/polymer and LCF remain candidates with cement
Final selection among remaining candidates is based on availability, economics, and other project factors

equations.description: Table 2-3 footnote (c), as printed: PI <= 20 + 50 - percent passing No. 200 (0.075 mm) sieve (cited by area 2C item 2; area 1C item 2 cites (b)); computed as PI <= 20 + (50 - percent passing No. 200 sieve)/4, the 2004 edition's Table 2-1 footnote b (printed 2-3)

tables: Table 2-3: Guide for Selecting a Stabilizing Additive
sections.applicability: Second half of the Figure 2-1 / Table 2-3 selection procedure; shows exactly how each stabilizer's restriction is checked against a specific soil.

sections.title: Fibers (Selection Guidance)
sections.summary: Fibers provide mechanical stabilization usable in many soil types, giving immediate improvements in load bearing and crack resistance. High-surface-area fibers (tape) suit fine-grained soils better; longer fibers improve performance but hamper construction/mixing.
sections.body: Fibers can be used in many soil types because they provide mechanical stabilization. Monofilament, tape, and fibrillated fibers are most common for improving soils. They provide immediate improvements in load bearing and crack resistance by enhancing strain resistance. Fibers mixed into soil without adhesives (i.e., cement) rely on mechanical interlock, friction, and fiber entanglement between themselves and soil particles to anchor the fiber in place. Thus, a high surface area fiber (such as a tape fiber) may be more efficient in a fine-grained clay soil than in a coarse-grained soil such as gravel, where fewer soil grains are in contact with the fiber. Longer fibers generally result in improved performance but hamper construction. They are more difficult to mix and considerable "balling" may occur, diminishing efficiency. After mixing, workability is sharply reduced, making blade work and grading difficult.
key_points: Fibers mixed into soil without adhesives rely on mechanical interlock, friction, and fiber entanglement
Tape fibers (high surface area) work better in fine-grained clay soils; fewer contacts in coarse gravel
Longer fibers improve performance but cause 'balling' and are harder to mix
Workability is sharply reduced after mixing, complicating blade work and grading
sections.applicability: Supplementary guidance for fiber selection layered on top of the Figure 2-1 / Table 2-3 primary additive choice.

sections.title: Use of Stabilized Soils in Frost Areas
sections.summary: Heading for 2-2.1 Frost Considerations, 2-2.2 Limitations and 2-2.3 Construction Cutoff Dates.
sections.body: [Printed as a heading only (p. 9); its text is under 2-2.1 Frost Considerations, 2-2.2 Limitations and 2-2.3 Construction Cutoff Dates.]
sections.applicability: Container section; see 2-2.1 through 2-2.3 for frost-area design and construction guidance.

sections.title: Frost Considerations
sections.summary: Pavements may see cyclic freeze-thaw (as the frost line advances/retreats) or heaving (quasi-equilibrium frost line enabling moisture migration and ice lens formation in frost-susceptible material). Bituminous, polymer, cement, lime, and LCF are the most common frost-area additives.
sections.body: Pavement systems may experience two general types of freeze-thaw action. Cyclic freeze-thaw occurs in the material when freezing occurs as the advancing frost line moves by and thawing subsequently occurs. Heaving conditions develop when a quasi-equilibrium frost line condition is established in the stabilized material layer. If the material is frost-susceptible, the static frost line situation provides favorable conditions for moisture migration and subsequent ice lens formation and heaving. While bituminous, polymer, portland cement, lime, and LCF stabilization are the most common additives, other stabilizers may be used for pavement construction in areas of frost design but only with approval from the Pavements DWG. Additives and cold weather placement techniques are also available for portland cement stabilization and are addressed in Chapter 4.
key_points: Cyclic freeze-thaw: repeated freezing/thawing as the frost line advances and retreats
Heaving: quasi-equilibrium frost line enables moisture migration and ice lens formation in frost-susceptible material
Most common frost-area additives: bituminous, polymer, portland cement, lime, LCF
Other stabilizers may be used in areas of frost design but only with approval from the Pavements DWG
sections.applicability: Applies to any pavement stabilization design sited in a seasonal-frost region.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: In frost areas, stabilized soil is used in one of the upper elements of a pavement only if the cost is justified by the reduced thickness. Use soil modification (a lower degree of additive) in frost areas only with caution and after intensive tests, since weakly cemented material usually endures repeated freezing and thawing less well; a possible exception is soil encapsulated in a membrane-encapsulated-soil-layer system. Do not stabilize soils to improve strength at the expense of making them more susceptible to ice segregation.
sections.body: In frost areas, stabilized soil is used in one of the upper elements of a pavement system only if the cost is justified by the reduced pavement thickness. Use a soil treatment with a lower degree of additive than that indicated for stabilization (i.e., soil modification) in frost areas only with caution and after intensive tests because weakly cemented material usually has less capacity to endure repeated freezing and thawing than firmly cemented material. A possible exception is modifying a soil that will be encapsulated within an impervious envelope as part of a membrane-encapsulated-soil-layer pavement system. A soil unsuitable for encapsulation due to excessive moisture migration and thaw weakening may be made suitable by moderate amounts of a stabilizing additive. Test modified materials to ascertain the desired improvement is durable through repeated freeze-thaw cycles. Do not stabilize soils to improve the strength at the expense of making the soil more susceptible to ice segregation.
key_points: In frost areas, stabilized soil is used in one of the upper elements of a pavement only if the cost is justified by the reduced pavement thickness
Use soil modification in frost areas only with caution and after intensive tests; weakly cemented material usually has less capacity to endure repeated freezing and thawing
A possible exception is modifying a soil encapsulated in an impervious envelope (membrane-encapsulated-soil-layer system)
Test modified materials to ascertain the improvement is durable through repeated freeze-thaw cycles
Do not stabilize soils to improve the strength at the expense of making the soil more susceptible to ice segregation
sections.applicability: Applies when deciding between full stabilization and lighter modification for frost-area pavement layers.

sections.title: Construction Cutoff Dates
sections.summary: Construct cement-, lime-, or LCF-stabilized materials early enough in the season to develop adequate strength before the first freezing cycle; strength gain is substantially lower at 50 degF than at 70 or 80 degF. In frost areas, set a construction cutoff date well in advance of freezing (e.g., 30 days), because a seven-day curing period is not adequate protection from freezing if the lime or cement reactions continue past it.
sections.body: Construct materials stabilized with cement, lime, or LCF early enough during the construction season to allow the development of adequate strength before the first freezing cycle begins. The rate of strength gain is substantially lower at 50 degF (10 degC) than at 70 degF or 80 degF (21 degC or 27 degC). Chemical reactions will not occur rapidly for (1) lime-stabilized soils when the soil temperature is less than 60 degF (16 degC) and is not expected to increase for one month or (2) cement-stabilized soils when the soil temperature is less than 40 degF (4 degC) and is not expected to increase for one month. In frost areas, set a construction cutoff date well in advance of the onset of freezing conditions (e.g., 30 days) because it is not adequate to protect the mixture from freezing during a seven-day curing period as required by the applicable guide specifications if the lime or cement reactions continue past the seven-day period.
key_points: The rate of strength gain is substantially lower at 50 degF (10 degC) than at 70 or 80 degF (21 or 27 degC)
Reactions will not occur rapidly for lime-stabilized soils when soil temperature is less than 60 degF (16 degC) and not expected to increase for one month
Reactions will not occur rapidly for cement-stabilized soils when soil temperature is less than 40 degF (4 degC) and not expected to increase for one month
In frost areas, set a construction cutoff date well in advance of the onset of freezing (e.g., 30 days)
sections.applicability: Applies to scheduling cement, lime, or LCF stabilization construction in seasonal-frost regions.

sections.title: Thickness Reduction for Base and Subbase Courses
sections.summary: Stabilized base/subbase materials qualify for reduced layer thickness if they meet gradation (Ch. 3), strength/durability (Tables 2-1, 2-2 for cement/lime/LF/LCF; UFC 3-260-02 for bitumen), or minimum 400 psi UCS for polymer emulsion.
sections.body: Ensure the stabilized base and subbase course materials meet the requirements of gradation, strength, and durability to qualify for reduced layer thickness design. Gradation requirements are presented in paragraphs 3-1 through 3-6 covering design with each type of stabilizer. Unconfined compressive strength and durability requirements for bases and subbases treated with cement, lime, lime-cement, lime-fly ash (LF), and LCF are indicated in Tables 2-1 and 2-2, respectively. For bituminous-stabilized materials to qualify for reduced thickness, ensure they meet strength requirements in UFC 3-260-02. Polymer emulsion materials qualify for reduced thickness when they meet a minimum unconfined compressive strength of 400 psi (2.76 MPa). Ensure all stabilized materials except those treated with bitumen and polymer emulsion meet minimum durability criteria to be used in pavement structures. There are no durability criteria for bituminous- or polymer emulsion-stabilized materials since it is assumed they will be waterproof if properly designed and constructed. [Table 2-1 (minimum unconfined compressive strength) and Table 2-2 (durability requirements) follow on the page; they are stored as tables.]
key_points: Ensure stabilized base and subbase materials meet the gradation (paragraphs 3-1 to 3-6), strength, and durability requirements to qualify for reduced layer thickness design
Cement/lime/LF/LCF: strength per Table 2-1 (table_2_1_min_ucs_requirements), durability per Table 2-2 (table_2_2_durability_requirements)
Bituminous-stabilized materials: meet the strength requirements in UFC 3-260-02; there are no durability criteria for them
Polymer emulsion materials qualify for reduced thickness at a minimum unconfined compressive strength of 400 psi (2.76 MPa); there are no durability criteria for them
Bitumen/polymer are assumed inherently waterproof if properly designed/constructed, hence no durability test requirement
tables: Table 2-1: Minimum Unconfined Compressive Strength for Cement-, Lime-, Lime-Cement, and Lime-Cement-Fly Ash-Stabilized Soils
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a project intends to use a stabilized layer's improved strength to reduce conventional pavement thickness (Appendix A procedure).

sections.title: Drying Wet Soils
sections.summary: Heading for 2-4.1 Chemicals, 2-4.2 Lime, 2-4.3 Amounts and 2-4.4 Factors.
sections.body: [Printed as a heading only (p. 11); its text is under 2-4.1 Chemicals, 2-4.2 Lime, 2-4.3 Amounts and 2-4.4 Factors.]
sections.applicability: Container section; see 2-4.1 through 2-4.4 for the chemistry, dosage, and rate-controlling factors of soil drying.

sections.title: Chemicals
sections.summary: Quicklime (calcium and magnesium oxides) reacts exothermically with water to form metal hydrates, evaporating additional moisture; this fast, exothermic reaction remains effective for drying soils down to freezing temperatures.
sections.body: The chemicals of choice for drying are oxides of calcium and magnesium, generally referred to as quicklime. Depending on the source, they may be further defined as high-calcium quicklime, magnesium quicklime, or dolomitic quicklime. These substances contain metal oxides (e.g., calcium oxide, CaO) that react with water to form the metal hydrate (e.g., CaO.(OH)2). As quicklime hydrates with water in the soil, it releases considerable heat (i.e., is exothermic), which in turn evaporates more water and further reduces the moisture content of the soil. Because this reaction is fast and exothermic, it is effective for drying soils down to freezing temperatures.
key_points: Quicklime types: high-calcium, magnesium, or dolomitic quicklime
Metal oxides (e.g., calcium oxide, CaO) react with water to form the metal hydrate; the heat released evaporates more water
Effective for drying soils even down to freezing temperatures due to the fast, exothermic reaction
sections.applicability: Basic chemistry underlying the wet-soil drying procedure; applies whenever quicklime is used as a drying agent.

sections.title: Lime (Drying Context)
sections.summary: Only quicklime is effective for drying; hydrated lime has already combined with water. 'Agricultural lime' has no engineering value. Any product with free CaO (portland cement, high-calcium fly ash, kiln dust) can serve as a drying agent.
sections.body: Lime is a generic term used to cover a variety of materials. Only quicklime is effective for drying soils. Hydrated lime has already combined with water and will not draw moisture into new chemical forms. It will have certain chemical reactions (cation exchange) with some clay minerals that will make them less plastic and easier to dry by conventional methods, but this is much different from the avid drying of quicklime that is not related to soil type. Be aware that "agricultural lime" has no value for engineering stabilization or drying uses. Do not construct stabilized soil materials using agricultural lime. Any product that contains free quicklime (CaO) can be used as a drying agent. The more CaO it contains, the more effective it will be as a drying agent. Portland cement, fly ash (particularly high calcium Class C ashes), and kiln dust are examples of common industrial materials with significant CaO content that can be used for soil drying. Their effectiveness for drying is directly dependent on their free CaO content. Quicklime is a caustic material; hence, normal safety precautions for such materials need to be followed (long sleeves and pants, rubber gloves, goggles, and mask). Quicklime is a relatively granular material and does not dust like the much finer hydrated lime. While safety precautions are required to handle this material, they are within the range of precautions used on construction sites. Quicklime is a commonly used industrial and construction material and the safety precautions required are reasonable to comply with in the field to ensure worker health and safety. Delivery is typically by dump truck and mixing is typically with a conventional field rotary mixer. Thorough mixing enhances uniform drying.
key_points: Only quicklime is effective for drying soils; hydrated lime has already combined with water and will not draw moisture into new chemical forms
"Agricultural lime" has no value for engineering stabilization or drying uses; do not construct stabilized soil materials using it
Any free-CaO product (portland cement, high-calcium Class C fly ash, kiln dust) can serve as a drying agent
Quicklime is caustic; follow normal safety precautions (long sleeves and pants, rubber gloves, goggles, and mask)
sections.applicability: Clarifies which lime-family products are actually effective drying agents, distinguishing from products with no engineering value.

sections.title: Amounts
sections.summary: Quicklime dosage for drying is generally determined by trial-and-error field testing (known wet-soil weight mixed with known quicklime amount, repeated at varying dosages); a qualitative assessment of such a test is generally all that is justified for military engineering applications.
sections.body: Amounts for use are generally by trial and error. Take a known weight of a wet soil sample and mix with a known amount of quicklime and see visually and texturally if it dries the wet soil sample. The reaction with CaO is quick and results will be evident very rapidly. Repeat but vary the amount of additive. This is a practical way to ascertain if non-quicklime materials such as portland cement, fly ash, or kiln dust have free CaO to be effective to dry the soil. A qualitative assessment of a simple test of this sort is generally all that is justified for military engineering applications. This will also provide a rough initial estimate of the amount of additive to use for drying.
key_points: Dosage determined by trial-and-error: mix known soil weight with known quicklime amount and observe drying
Reaction is fast, so results are evident quickly, enabling rapid iteration
Same trial method screens whether portland cement/fly ash/kiln dust have enough free CaO to be effective
A qualitative field assessment is generally sufficient for military engineering applications
sections.applicability: Field procedure for estimating the required quicklime dosage on a specific wet soil.

sections.title: Factors
sections.summary: Three factors govern soil drying with quicklime: chemical hydration of CaO, exothermic-reaction-driven evaporation, and normal ambient evaporation -- so exact dosage formulas aren't justified; use multiple incremental additions toward the target moisture content.
sections.body: Three factors are involved with drying of the soil: chemical hydration of CaO, exothermic-reaction-caused evaporation, and normal evaporation because of ambient conditions. Therefore, trying to assign exact formulas for how much quicklime to add to gain a specific reduction in moisture content is not justified. It is better to make multiple additions to close in on the desired moisture content. One to two percent quicklime for each percent reduction in desired moisture content is a good starting point. [Table 2-3, Guide for Selecting a Stabilizing Additive, follows at the end of the chapter; it is stored as a table.]
key_points: Three drying mechanisms: chemical hydration of CaO, exothermic-reaction evaporation, and normal ambient evaporation
No exact formula is justified for quicklime dosage vs. moisture reduction -- multiple incremental additions are recommended instead
Rule-of-thumb starting point: 1-2% quicklime per 1% desired moisture-content reduction
sections.applicability: Explains why the drying procedure is iterative/trial-based rather than formula-based; sets the practical dosage starting point.
